The defendants aggrieved by a decree of injunction restraining them from obstructing the plaintiffs'
right of easement have come up in this second appeal challenging the concurrent findings rendered by the Principal Munsiff's Court, Ernakulam in OS No.232/2014 and confirmed by the II Additional Sub Court, Ernakulam in AS No.30/2017 .

2. The brief facts necessary for the disposal of the appeal are as follows:
Plaint A item No.1 scheduled property having an extent of 20 cents belongs to the 1st plaintiff.
Plaint A item No.2 property consisting of 20 cents belongs to the 2nd plaintiff.
The properties were derived by settlement deed No.414/76 dated 13.2.1976 of SRO, Ernakulam.
1.25 Acres of land towards the North and Eastern sides of plaint A item Nos.1 and 2 belong to the brother of the plaintiffs, one Vincent.
The properties were given to Vincent by the father of the plaintiffs by 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 document No.1875/68 of SRO, Ernakulam dated 30.8.1968.
When the aforesaid property was settled in favour of Vincent, it was made clear that a pathway having a width of 8 links will be provided to access the property stated as A schedule to the plaint.
It is contended that after setting apart the 8 links wide pathway, the balance property alone is vested with Vincent.
Later, it was mutually agreed that certain portions of the property from item Nos.1 & 2 of A schedule will also be set apart for widening of the existing pathway by consent deed dated 9.2.2008.
It is contended that contrary to the said consent deed, the 1st defendant, after setting apart the property scheduled as B schedule to the plaint, has constructed a compound wall.
Thereafter, he constructed a compound wall on the Eastern and Western sides of his property.
The land which is set apart to be used as the way by the 1st defendant is after recognising the wish of his father as per the deed No.1875/68.
While so, there was an attempt by the defendants to demolish the compound wall towards the Southern end and annex B schedule way into their own property.
Accordingly, stating the cause of action arisen on 20.2.2014, the suit was instituted.

During the pendency of the suit, an amendment was sought to amend the B schedule pathway having an extent of 19 metres in length and 3 metres 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 in width, which was allowed.
The defendants entered appearance and resisted the suit denying the right of the plaintiffs, contending that there existed no pathway having an extent of 2.13 metres width, equivalent to 7 feet.
The execution of the consent deed dated 9.2.2008 was also denied.
The existence of the B schedule pathway being used by the plaintiffs to enter into the Chammany Road in order to access the Chittoor-Cheranalloor Road was denied by the defendants.

Equally so, the claim for easement by prescription was also denied.
The claim for easement by grant was also questioned as no evidence was produced by the plaintiffs to show that there existed a pathway as claimed by them.

Defendants further contended that it is not a compound wall constructed but a temporary embankment like much within their property, to temporarily avoid building material being washed off by ingress of river water.
On behalf of the plaintiffs, Exts.A1 to A5 documents were produced and PW1 to PW6 were examined.
On behalf of the defendants, Exts.B1 to B5 documents were produced and DW1 was examined.
Exts. X1
to X2 are third-party exhibits.
Exts.C1 & C2 are the advocate commissioner's report and the sketch.

The trial court on the basis of the pleadings of both parties, framed the following issues:
2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 "1.
Whether
plaint B schedule pathway is in existence?
2. Whether plaintiffs acquired right of easement as claimed to use plaint B schedule pathway?
3. Whether plaintiffs are entitled to get decree of permanent prohibitory injunction as prayed for?
4. What is the order as to costs?"
On appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence, the existence of a right of easement by grant as well as a claim for easement by prescription were found by the trial court.

Accordingly, the suit was decreed restraining the defendants from annexing the portion of B schedule way and portion of eastern public road to their property by demolishing the eastern and southern compound wall of property covered by Ext.B2.
They were also restrained from obstructing the plaintiffs to access the property through B schedule pathway including vehicular access.
Aggrieved, the defendants preferred AS No.30/2017 before the first appellate court.

The first appellate court, on reappreciation of evidence, found that the entitlement of the plaintiffs is an easement by grant and therefore, dismissed the appeal affirming the findings of the trial court regarding the entitlement for a decree for prohibitory injunction.

As against the dismissal of the appeal, the defendants have come up with the present second appeal raising the 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 following substantial question of law framed by this Court on 11.4.2018:
"When in Exhibit A1 - the deed of transfer in favour of the plaintiffs 1 & 2 by their predecessors of plaint A schedule items 1 & 2 properties and when the 1st plaintiff has transferred plaint A schedule item 1 in favour of 3rd plaintiff by Exhibit B5 also there is absolutely no pathway provided in the east of the plaintiffs properties and Exhibit A2 by which defendants father purchased property, there is only a permission stated to be given to transferor in Exhibit A1, and admittedly even in 2013 there is no such pathway, have not the courts below gone wrong in law in not holding that there is no such pathway as claimed as Plaint B schedule and by no means there is any such right Sherif Vincent vs M.C.Stephen on 29 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/118954845/
4 even over 8 links available as easement by grant in favour of the plaintiffs?"

Before proceeding with this case, this Court must notice certain compelling facts and developments which have taken place during the course of the hearing of the appeal.

On 11.9.2025, this Court passed a detailed order by which certain concessions made by the learned counsel for the appellants were recorded and the case was adjourned to 18.9.2025.
But, on 18.9.2025 when the matter was taken up for further consideration

Though this Court was not inclined to grant further time, 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 especially since the arguments were complete, but since the respondents had changed their counsel during the mid-way of the appeal, just after the conclusion of the arguments of both sides,

6. Since the parties were given more than one opportunity to settle the issues once and for all,
considering the fact that they were relatives, this Court waited till today to see whether an amicable solution to the dispute could be arrived at.
But then, since the parties are bent upon litigating the matter, this Court is constrained to take up the matter on the merits.
7. Sri

.M.P.Ramnath, the learned counsel appearing for the appellants, raised various submissions touching upon the sustainability of the findings rendered by the trial court as affirmed by the first appellate court.

The thrust of the argument of Sri.M.P.Ramnath, the learned counsel appearing for the appellants, revolved around the finding of the courts below regarding the 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 existence of an easement by grant.

The learned counsel would point out that the basic case set up by the plaintiffs in the suit is as regards the existence of an 8 links wide way, which later transformed into a three metres wide pathway equivalent to a 10 feet.
However, it was subsequently amended on 22.6.2016 by enlarging the extent up to 19 metres in length and 3 metres in width.
He would further submit that though in paragraph No.3 of the plaint, it is asserted that there existed a consent deed between the parties on 9.2.2008, the same did not see the light of day.
Therefore, the contention of the plaintiffs that both the plaintiffs and defendants had given a certain extent of property for carving out of the pathway is completely baseless.
He would further submit that the plea of easement by grant and the plea of easement by prescription are mutually destructive.
In order to prove the existence of a right of easement, it is necessary that the plaintiffs should prove the existence of the pathway in question.

In support of his contention, relied on the decision of this Court in Raveendran v. Lohithakshan [2017 (2) KLT 865], wherein this Court had categorically held that the property over which the easement is claimed should be clearly identifiable as per the description of the plaint.

He further relied on the decision of this Court in Madhavan 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 v. Narayanankutti [2019 (4) KLT 208].
8.

KLT 431] and the Single Bench decisions of this Court in Maniyan Krishnan and Anr v. Maniyan Nanukuttan [AIR 1986 Ker 75] & Thottathil Thamasikkum Cherootty alias Balan v. Puliyaratharayil Velayudhan Nair [AIR 1998 Ker 164].

He would further submit that, going by the additional documents produced by way of an application,
I.A.No.5549/2017, by the appellants before the first appellate court, the existence of the B schedule pathway cannot be found out.
With specific reference to the survey sketch, the learned counsel pointed out that there was no pathway as claimed as B schedule.

Before concluding, the learned counsel would submit that the first appellate 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 court erred egregiously in rejecting the said application and refusing to accept the additional documents, which were only certified copies of public documents.

He would finally point out that, once the first Sherif Vincent vs M.C.Stephen on 29 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/118954845/
6 appellate court had concluded that a claim for prescription is not maintainable as far as the plaintiffs are concerned, the first appellate court could not have concluded that there is an easement by grant, especially since for establishing an easement by grant, a right has to be conferred by a specific document.
9.

Per contra, Sri.T.N.Manoj, the learned counsel appearing for the respondents/plaintiffs,
countered the submissions of Sri.M.P.Ramnath by contending that in a case of easement, it is not necessary that there should be a declaration of right.
If a complaint regarding obstruction of an easementary right is made out, then, a simple suit for injunction is maintainable and that the courts are bound to grant the relief.

In support of his contention, relied on the decision of this Court in Unnikrishnan v. Ponnu Ammal [1999 KHC 93] and the decision of the Supreme Court in Sree Swayam Prakash Ashramam and Another v. G.Anandavally Amma and Others [2010 (1) KHC 232].

sentences.text: He would further point out that the concurrent findings of the fact entered by the courts below do not 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 call for interference in terms of Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

At any rate, the learned counsel justified the clients' stand of not accepting the settlement offered by the learned counsel appearing for the appellants/defendants, since,
according to him, the claim is based on a justifiable cause.
10. In reply, the learned counsel appearing for the appellants would point out that for making out the case of easement by grant, necessarily, there should be a specific conferment of the said right.
Neither Ext.A1 settlement deed nor any subsequent document make out a case for easement by grant.
At best, Ext.A2 could only be construed as a permission to use the pathway in question, which will not ripen into any right.

At any rate, when the first appellate court confined its finding to easement by grant and disallowed the claim of prescription, the plaintiffs ought to have questioned the same in a separate appeal or at least by preferring a cross appeal.

He would thus conclude by contending that the courts below failed to notice the impact of Section 47 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, which provides for termination of the easement by grant if there is a discontinuation in the usage for nearly 20 years.

He further submitted that the affirmation of the prohibitory decree granted by the trial court 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 is contrary to Section 35 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, which provides that an injunction could be granted only with regard to the obstruction to the right of easement and not beyond the same.
11. I have considered the rival submissions raised across the bar and perused the judgments rendered by the courts below and the records of the present case.

12. Though it appears that this Court has framed a solitary substantial question of law, in fact, the question is a multi-faceted one, which requires this Court to determine;
(a) Whether there is an easement by grant in Exts.A1 and B5 documents by which the 1st plaintiff and the 3rd plaintiff were conferred with the right title and interest over the plaint item A schedule property.
( b) Whether by a mere mentioning of a right granted by the defendants' father when Ext.A2 was executed, a right of easement by grant could be made out?

Sherif Vincent vs M.C.Stephen on 29 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/118954845/
7

(c) The failure of the plaintiffs to prove the existence of the B schedule pathway, which runs contrary to the extent of the pathway provided under Ext.A2, could sustain the findings of the courts below.

2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 Thus, in effect, this Court is required to answer three substantial questions of law.
13.
Before venturing to answer these questions, this Court is required to address one more issue.

An additional substantial question of law was framed as to whether the judgments of the trial court and the first appellate court could be sustained on the failure of the plaintiffs to carry out the amendment ordered as per order dated 21.6.2016 in IA No.3309/2016.

However, later, on perusal of the files, it is seen that instead of carrying out the amendment in the original plaint, the plaintiffs had carried out the amendment in the duplicate copy of the plaint in terms of the order dated 21.6.2016.
Therefore, having found that the plaintiffs have carried out the amendment, the said substantial question of law is required to be answered in negative against the appellants.
14. Coming to the larger questions raised before this Court, one needs to carefully consider the exact purport of Ext.A2 document in order to find out whether an easement by grant is made out or not.

Before going into the said issue, this Court must notice the fact that normally when an easement by grant is claimed, the plaintiffs or defendants would necessarily put up the claim based on their 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 respective documents of title.

But then, in the present case,
neither under Ext.A1 by which the first plaintiff was conferred the right, title and interest nor under Ext.B5 by which the 3rd plaintiff was conferred the right, title and interest over item No.2 of the plaint A schedule, any right of easement over plaint B schedule is mentioned.
The Indian Easements Act does not define how and in what manner an easement by grant is to be made out, nor there is a clear definition regarding such a right.

Therefore, when we proceed to consider the true purport of the words easement by grant, necessarily, it must be remembered that the right claimed by plaintiffs or the defendants must be based on something which is reduced into writing.
Ideally, the document by which right, title and interest over the property is claimed must mention such right.
It is also possible to enter into a separate contract conferring such rights.
15. It is the fundamental principle of easement law that every easement is, in theory, rooted in a grant.
The manner in which such a grant is made differs from case to case.
Pertinently, Indian law clearly permits the acquisition of easements by implied grant.
That is, an easement may arise by implication, and the intention to grant can be inferred either from the terms of the grant or from the surrounding 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 circumstances.

Though easement by grant is (generally) said to have arisen from a 'contract', the provisions of law that deal with the matter do not specifically require 'consideration' in the creation of easements by grant.
16. An easement by grant arises from an agreement or contract between parties and is a legal right attached to the land, not a personal privilege.

It can be created either Expressly: Through clear language in a deed or other legal instrument or Impliedly: Inferred from the surrounding circumstances when a property is transferred Sherif Vincent vs M.C.Stephen on 29 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/118954845/
8 17.

sentences.text: But then, the larger question is whether there is an easement by grant in the present case.
One must remember that, what was claimed by the plaintiffs is a prescriptive right as well as a right by grant.
It is a different aspect, as to whether both claims will go simultaneously or not.
But then, this Court is relieved of deciding the issue in view of the finding of the first appellate court that the respondents/plaintiffs can only claim easement by grant.
Admittedly, the plaintiffs did not choose to file a cross appeal challenging the findings against them by the first appellate court.

18. As stated above, admittedly, there is no contract between the appellants and the respondents herein or their predecessors 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 through which the respondents/plaintiffs can claim the right of easement by grant.

Indisputably, the plaintiffs claim is built on the contents of Ext.A2 which speaks about providing an 8 links way to access the plaintiffs'
property.
It must be remembered that Ext.A2 is a settlement deed executed in favour of the father of the 1st appellant/1st defendant .
Therefore, it passes one's comprehension as to how the plaintiffs claim of a grant could be upheld under Ext.A2.

At best, what could be construed from Ext.A2 is a permission to access the way having 8 links provided by the seller in favour of the father of the 1 st defendant, so that the plaintiffs' predecessor could have access to their property.

19. The fact that in Ext.A2, there is a mention regarding the permission granted to the plaintiffs'
predecessor to access the public road through the 8 links way, destroys the entire edifice of the plaint claim.
One cannot fathom the reasoning behind the claim when, what is granted is a permission to access the 8 links way.
This Court fails to see as to how a permissive right would ripen to an easement by grant.
The usage of the word 'permission' is sufficient indication to conclude that what is granted is only a licence and not an easement by grant.

Perhaps, the seller of father of the 1st defendant, could have likely 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 included the clause in Ext.A2,
to explicitly prevent the other neighbours from claiming right over the pathway.
This foresight ensured that the use was temporary and non-binding and that his successor would not be burdened by a permanent easement.
Apart from that, this Court could not see any plausible reason as to why there was a necessity to mention about the permissive right to use the 8 links way when Ext.A2 document was executed.

20. But when the plaintiffs instituted the suit, they tried to enlarge the scope of their permissive right, by setting up a claim that the pathway in question has over the years changed its character and assumed the nature of public way.
The falsity of the case set up by the plaintiffs is writ large on the records, and also in the light of the evidence adduced by the parties, including Exts.X1 and X2 documents summoned.

The plaintiffs categorically asserted that during the passage of time, the 8 links wide pathway was widened enough to transform itself into a 3 metres width and 19 metres length pathway by the efflux of time and also through an agreement dated 9.2.2008.
However, the plaintiffs failed to produce the said agreement and the moment the plaintiffs failed to produce the said agreement, the trial court should have drawn an adverse inference; but

rather, this Court 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 is surprised by the fact that the trial court took extraneous efforts to hold that the B schedule pathway had been identified and a right of easement by both grant and prescription is made out.

The extent of deviation of the plaintiffs' case is evident from the fact that during the pendency of the suit, an attempt was made to establish their right over the B schedule pathway as one having a public character and maintained by the Panchayat as a public Sherif Vincent vs M.C.Stephen on 29 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/118954845/
9 way.

Be that as it may, this Court need not delve into the said issue, inasmuch as the findings of the courts below are not centered around the question as to whether the B schedule is a public pathway or not.
21. The 1st plaintiff was extensively cross-
examined on the plaint claim.
He deposed that when Ext.B5 settlement deed was executed in favour of the 3rd plaintiff, B schedule pathway was not in existence.
In Ext.A1 also, there is no mention of any such pathway claimed as B schedule.
It is only later that the plaintiffs found out that there was a way which got mentioned in Ext.A2.
He would further assert in his oral testimony that what is claimed in the plaint is only the pathway, which has been set apart in Ext.A2 and nothing else and nothing more.

In the light of these categoric admission, this Court fails to comprehend as to how the trial court could conclude that the 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 plaintiffs have probabilised their right of way over plaint B schedule and the existence of B schedule with cogent and convincing evidence.

22. The extent of impropriety that stems out from the findings of the trial court is evident from the fact that the trial court, on analysing the evidence of the plaintiffs and construction of Ext.A2,
concluded that though Ext.A2 prescribes an easement by grant, actually the plaintiffs have got a right by prescription.

This Court cannot but notice the extent of inconsistency in the finding,
especially since the trial court had travelled beyond the claim of the plaintiffs and found that the claim of easement by prescription is sustainable.

23. In Kallen Devi v. Raghavan [2012 (3) KLT 142], this Court considered the question as to whether a plea of easement by prescription and grant will go together and concluded that both are mutually destructive.
24. The finding of the first appellate court is more intriguing.
The first appellate court on the construction of Ext.A2 concluded that, Ext.A2 confers only an easement by grant and not prescription.

If that be so, the entire edifice of the case set up by the plaintiffs collapses because there is admittedly no correlation between the extent of property scheduled as B schedule to the plaint as well as the extent of 2025:KER:73769 RSA NO. 418 OF 2018 property over which the alleged right of easement is granted under Ext.A2.Therefore
, this Court cannot but conclude that the plaintiffs claim for easement by grant must necessarily fail.

25. Yet another facet of the finding rendered by the trial court which requires this Court to take note of the extraneous considerations which passed on to the minds of the court is as regards the grant of prohibitory injunction against the appellants.
One need not have to travel much to understand the impropriety in the manner in which the finding was rendered by the trial court.
It is trite law, that in a claim for right of easement, the scope of injunction is confined to the right claimed.
Section 35 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 reads as under.
"35. Injunction to restrain disturbance.--
